At the police office in Saint-Charles station
27 December. Ioana and Julien are waiting for their train back to Lyon at Saint-Charles station in Marseille. Suddenly Ioana can’t find her phone. They go to the station’s police officer.
My phone’s been stolen! Ten minutes ago, on the platform.
All right. Tell me everything, calmly. What were you doing?
I was sitting on a bench. I was waiting for the train and reading a message from my mother.
I was buying sandwiches at the café next door.
Suddenly a man came up. He asked me the time. I put my phone down on the bench to look at my watch…
And while you were looking at your watch, he took the phone.
Exactly! He left very fast towards the exit. I shouted, but he ran.
Can you describe him? What did he look like?
He was quite tall and slim. He was about thirty, I think. He had dark hair and a short beard.
He was wearing a black jacket, jeans and a red cap. And he had a grey rucksack.
A red cap… Wait. (He speaks into the radio.) … Madam, you’re lucky. My colleagues stopped a man with a red cap at the exit five minutes ago.
It was in his rucksack, with four other phones. You just need to report the theft and sign here.
Thank you, sir! Lucky you were here. But our train leaves in ten minutes!
someone (“on m’a volé” = something of mine was stolen)
about thirty (“une trentaine d’années” = about 30 years old)
to carry (“porter plainte” = to report a crime)
“Qu’est-ce qui” = “kes-KEE”, “qu’est-ce que” = “kes-KUH”. Both mean “what”, but “qui” when “what” is the subject (what happened?) and “que” when it’s the object (what are you doing?).
Les yeux = “lay-ZYUH” (liaison with z!), un œil = “ẽ-NUHY”. The singular and plural look nothing alike.
Tranquille, ville, mille are read with an “l”: “trã-KEEL”, “veel”, “meel”. But fille, famille, travailler with a “y”. Exceptions to learn by heart.
Gros = “gro” (silent s), grosse = “gros” (s heard). As with all adjectives: the feminine makes the final consonant heard.
In “ils portaient” the ending -aient is silent (“por-TEH”), but in “heureusement”, “calmement” the -ment is heard: “uh-ruhz-MÃ”.
1. Setting and events: imparfait + passé composé
A story usually has two layers. The imparfait paints the SETTING (what was going on, what things were like), and the passé composé brings in the EVENTS (what suddenly happened, once).

Think of a film: the imparfait is the background (the camera rolls slowly), the passé composé is the action (something suddenly happens). Like English: “I was waiting for the train (background) when a man came up (action).”
The typical mistake: everything in the passé composé. “J’ai été sur un banc, j’ai attendu le train…” sounds like a list of facts, not a story. Descriptions go in the imparfait.
I was waiting for the train when a man came up. (action in progress + interruption)
While you were looking at your watch, he took the phone.
While Julien was buying the sandwiches, Ioana was reading. (two parallel actions → both in the imparfait)
“Pendant que” (while) almost always introduces an imparfait. “Pendant” without “que” + noun = “during”: pendant les vacances, pendant deux heures.
For physical description French uses two verbs: ÊTRE (for general features) and AVOIR (for body parts). In stories, both go in the imparfait.
Il est grand / petit / de taille moyenne.
Il a les cheveux courts / longs / bruns / blonds / gris.
Elle est mince / un peu ronde.
Elle a les yeux bleus / verts / marron.
Il a une barbe / une moustache / des lunettes.
Il a une trentaine d’années (≈ 30 years old).
Hair and eyes take the definite article: “Il a LES cheveux bruns” (he has dark hair), “Elle a LES yeux verts”. Not “ses cheveux”.
“Porter” = to wear (clothes): “Il portait une veste noire et une casquette rouge.”
Approximate age: une vingtaine / trentaine / quarantaine / cinquantaine d’années = about 20 / 30 / 40 / 50 years old.
You’ve learnt “on” = “we” (spoken). But “on” also means “someone, people” (an unspecified subject). English often uses the passive or “they” here:
My phone’s been stolen. / Someone stole my phone.
Un jour… / Ce matin-là… / Il y a deux jours…
One day… / That morning… / Two days ago…
What happened? “Qu’est-ce qui s’est passé ?” It’s what the police officer, the doctor or a worried friend asks.

He left very fast towards the exit.
It was the beginning of January. It was cold and there was fog over the Saône.
One evening Ioana was coming home from work when she noticed a man in front of her building.
He was quite old. He was wearing a long grey coat and a black hat. He had a big white moustache.
He didn’t move. He was looking at the windows of the building, very carefully.
The next day the man was there again, at the same time, in the same place. And the day after too.
Madame Bernard was worried. “He’s looking at my flat! Maybe he’s a burglar. He’s waiting for the right moment…”
Victor wasn’t scared at all. He was sleeping on the radiator, as usual.
On the fourth evening Ioana decided to talk to the man. She went down with Julien. They were a little scared.
“Excuse me, sir. Are you waiting for someone?”
The man jumped. Then he smiled and opened his coat. Underneath he was holding a big sketchbook.
“Sorry, I frightened you! I’m a painter. I draw the old houses of Lyon at sunset.”
In the sketchbook there was a magnificent drawing of their building. You could see all the windows, the balconies, the flowers…
And on one balcony there was a little ginger cat asleep. It was Victor!
“I grew up in this building,” the man explained. “When I was a child, I lived on the third floor. There was always a cat on that balcony.”
Madame Bernard arrived at that moment. She looked at the man for a long time. Then she cried: “Paul? Little Paul Martin?”
It was the little boy of the former neighbours, who used to play on the stairs fifty years ago!
That evening they all had tea at Madame Bernard’s, and Paul gave her his drawing. Today it hangs in the living room, above Victor’s radiator.
